text:
Happy Veterans Day! It's a gray, quiet one, mostly cloudy and chilly, with a high near 46. The European model and one TV forecast are a few degrees warmer, so upper 40s isn't out of the question. Tonight settles into the 30s, around 33 by morning.

Thursday is the day to plan around. A few sprinkles are possible at dawn, but the steadier rain holds off until early afternoon. It ramps up from about 1 and peaks around 3 or 4, with roughly a quarter inch by the time it's done. The high is near 44. It's a marginal setup, so Burlington stays mostly rain with maybe some wet flakes mixed in after dark. The forecasters are confident about a real snow event for the hills, but at lake level I'd expect slush on the grass at most.

Friday stays damp and raw, with highs in the upper 30s to low 40s. Saturday morning is the coldest, in the 20s, so expect frost. Warmer and quieter next week.

Take the umbrella and a warm layer Thursday, and get outdoor errands done before lunch.

Looks like a stray rain or snow shower possible until early afternoon, otherwise mostly cloudy with a high near 43.
Looks like some sun returns Monday, partly sunny and dry with a high near 44, a nice break after the wet stretch.
Trending mostly sunny and dry Tuesday with a high near 45, a pleasant finish to the week.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: A gradually deepening surface low will track from the Ohio Valley east over southern New England before heading off into the Canadian Maritimes on Thursday into Friday. Despite a favorable storm track for snow, a marginally cold initial airmass will be in place at the onset, especially at the surface due to a lack of Canadian high pressure to the north. Precipitation looks to enter southwestern areas Thursday morning but very slowly make its way northeast during the day. By Thursday night, it should reach the Northeast Kingdom, but the heaviest rates may remain to the south. At the onset, surface temperatures will likely be in the 30s in most places, with low 40s possible in the warmest valleys. Steep lapse rates will exist with summit levels well below freezing, though a lack of a significantly dry layer will prevent significant wet-bulb cooling. Precipitation will begin as rain in the valleys and snow at the summits. A first estimate of initial snow levels is around 1,500 ft. Light rates and daytime occurrence will prevent significant accumulations at the onset outside the mountains. A weak November sun angle will limit some of the warming effects though. Heading into Thursday night, heavier rates will likely enter the region, and darkness will end any solar radiation. The combination of lowering temperatures due to dynamical cooling and nighttime cooling will allow snow levels to drop a bit, and especially allow for more efficient accumulations at higher elevations with higher snow ratios. By Friday morning, snow levels should be around or below 1,000 ft. While brief periods of snow are possible in the low valleys like the Champlain Valley and Lower Connecticut Valley, temperatures may stay just above freezing and prevent accumulations other than some slush in grassy-type surfaces. As the low tracks to the east heading through Friday, cyclonic northwest flow will develop and maintain some upslope snow showers in the higher terrain into Saturday. Boundary layer temperatures will reach their lowest values Saturday morning, with most areas likely seeing temperatures in the 20s. Warm Lake Champlain temperatures will probably further limit the already marginal accumulations in the immediate Champlain Valley, especially with northwest flow off the lake and downsloping along the eastern Adirondacks. Overall, this is still a relatively low-confidence forecast. Our deterministic most-likely scenario has snow amounts in the 3-6 inch range for areas around and above 2,000 ft. One exception is northern Vermont, where the heaviest bands may not reach. Areas between 1,000- 2,000 ft look to be in the 1-3 inch range, and below 1,000 ft looks to be a slushy coating. However, the ensemble spread is still massive. The NBM 10th percentile is 2-4 inches above 2,000 ft and the 90th percentile is 10-18 inches. Deterministic models are all split. WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) -Happy Wednesday! Today is another rather gray and cloudy day for most, but there could be a few breaks of sunshine especially south through the first half of the day. Temperatures for the day climb back into the 40s for this afternoon. Through the night ahead, rain showers and mountain snow showers begin to make their arrival into southern Vermont pushing northward into central Vermont overnight. Overnight lows fall back into the 30s for most. A few mixed showers could linger through Friday and even into Saturday, but I think accumulation is rather limited. Temperatures for both days are on the cooler side only in the 30s and struggling to reach the lower 40s in the broader valley locations. We trend drier and nicer into the start of next week. Sunday still features more clouds than sun, but we are a few degrees warmer in the upper 30s and lower 40s for most. By Monday we look to get a tad more sunshine going with temperatures remaining rather stable. Tuesday for now looks to feature even more sunshine, and temperatures in the low to mid 40s.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-11T00:10:00Z — same caveat): Rain and snow on the way Thursday into Friday — Wednesday (Veterans Day) looks mostly dry, with only a spot shower or flurry possible. However, it will be mostly cloudy and chilly, with highs in the upper 40s. The late-week stretch looks quite chilly, as the jet stream dips farther south. Highs only reach the low to mid-40s, with lots of clouds. Rain and elevation snow showers develop Thursday, especially by afternoon, as an area of low pressure approaches. Depending on the storm track, a period of steadier rain and mountain snow is possible Friday, with mixed showers lingering into Saturday. Several inches of snow will fall in some parts of the region, higher up. Drier weather is likely early next week, followed by a warmup into the 50s.
